prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Clobber game on a 5x6 grid. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(you: list[int], opponent: list[int]) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - Board size is 5 rows x 6 columns. - `you` and `opponent` are 5x6 arrays describing the board. - Values are 0 or 1. - `you[row, col] == 1` means you have a piece at cell `(row, col)`. - `opponent[row, col] == 1` means the opponent has a piece at cell `(row, col)`. - For any `(row, col)`, at most one of `you[row, col]` and `opponent[row, col]` is 1. # Action / Return Format - Return a string move in the format `'row,col,dir'`. - `row` is the row of the starting cell (0-4). - `col` is the column of the starting cell (0-5). - `dir` is the direction of the move: `'U'` (up), `'R'` (right), `'D'` (down), `'L'` (left). - The start cell must contain your piece. - The destination cell must be in bounds and contain an opponent piece. - A legal move must capture an adjacent opponent piece by moving one square orthogonally onto it. - The opponent piece is removed; your piece occupies the destination square; your starting square becomes empty. - The first player to have no legal moves on their turn loses. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
Given the 30-cell board, full search from the start is likely too slow, so I'm planning iterative deepening negamax with alpha-beta pruning, a transposition table, and move ordering within a strict time budget, falling back to mobility-based heuristics early on and full search once the board thins out. I'm also considering decomposing the position into independent components as the game progresses to speed up endgame analysis.

I'll represent the board as two 30-bit masks for each player with precomputed neighbor lists to generate moves quickly. For evaluation I'm leaning toward mobility difference (my available moves minus opponent's) as the core heuristic, with terminal positions scored as an immediate loss for the side with no legal moves, and I'm budgeting about 0.85 seconds per move given Python's node throughput.

For search I'll use negamax with alpha-beta pruning and a transposition table keyed on board state plus depth, run through iterative deepening so I always have a usable best move from the last completed depth even if time runs out mid-search. Move ordering will rely on the transposition table's best move first, then fall back to a cheap heuristic since fully evaluating each child's mobility for ordering is too expensive except at shallow depths.

I'm computing mobility efficiently using bitwise shifts across the 5x6 grid, counting how many of my pieces have an adjacent opponent piece in each of the four directions using bit_count for speed.

For terminal states, I want a no-moves loss to score as strongly negative but adjusted by depth so quicker wins/slower losses are preferred. I'll use a transposition table keyed by position, fresh per call, and skip partizan decomposition since it's too complex for this—sticking with plain alpha-beta.

Setting up the board representation with bitmask constants for rows, columns, and edge masks...

Verifying the up/down shifts work correctly with the bit boundaries, then I'm planning move generation by iterating over each set bit in me's bitboard using precomputed neighbor direction lists per index.

For negamax, I'm sketching node counting with periodic timeout checks, transposition table lookups, terminal detection when no moves remain (loss), and depth-limited evaluation falling back to mobility scoring.

At the root, I'll use iterative deepening keeping track of the best move so far, with a safe fallback to the first legal move if a timeout hits unexpectedly early. For move ordering, I want transposition table hits searched first, then remaining moves sorted by a cheap one-ply mobility estimate at deeper nodes, plus killer move heuristics to improve pruning.

Setting the time budget to about 0.85 seconds accounts for negligible Python startup overhead. I also need to handle the board input robustly, converting cells to plain ints in case it comes in as a numpy array rather than nested lists, before finalizing the code.
